passage:
Paragraph A
The Pacific Ocean covers a third of the surface of the earth. Scattered across it are islands so small and so far apart that finding one from another has been described as harder than finding a particular grain of sand on a beach. Yet by the time European ships arrived in the eighteenth century, almost every habitable island had been settled, some of them two thousand years earlier. The people who did this carried no compass, no chart and no instrument of any kind.

Paragraph B
European explorers could not account for it. The prevailing view for two centuries was that the islands must have been reached by accident — canoes blown off course, survivors washing ashore. This explanation was comfortable because it required no skill on the part of the islanders, but it never fitted the evidence. Settlement had proceeded largely eastward, against the prevailing winds and currents. Accidental drift would have moved people the other way.

Paragraph C
What the navigators actually used was a system built entirely on observation and memory. Its foundation was the star compass: a mental map of the points on the horizon where particular stars rise and set. Because a star rises at the same bearing every night, a sequence of them appearing in turn through the night gives a continuous direction to steer by. A navigator might hold thirty or more such bearings in memory, together with the order in which the stars appear.

Paragraph D
Stars fail in daylight and in cloud, so other cues carried the canoe between them. Ocean swells, generated by distant weather systems, run in consistent directions for days at a time; a navigator lying in the hull could feel the pitch and roll and hold a course by it. The colour and shape of clouds indicated land beyond the horizon, since islands generate their own cloud. Certain birds fly out to fish at dawn and return at dusk, so their direction at the right hour points towards land. Navigators in the Marshall Islands went further and built physical models of the sea, tying curved strips of palm rib together to show how swells bend around an island and where two swell patterns cross. These charts were not carried aboard. They were memorised on shore and left behind, since their purpose was to teach the pattern rather than to be consulted at sea.

Paragraph E
The most sophisticated element was a technique sometimes translated as the moving island. Rather than picture the canoe travelling towards a fixed destination, the navigator imagined the canoe stationary and a reference island, off to one side and often out of sight, moving past it against the star bearings. Tracking that imagined movement gave a continuous estimate of progress. It amounts to dead reckoning performed without written figures.

Paragraph F
The knowledge was transmitted orally over years of apprenticeship, usually within families, and it very nearly disappeared. Colonial administrations discouraged long voyages; engines and charts made the old methods unnecessary. By the 1970s only a handful of practising navigators remained, most of them on Satawal and neighbouring islands in Micronesia.

Paragraph G
It survived because of a deliberate revival. In 1976 a double-hulled canoe built to traditional design sailed from Hawaii to Tahiti, more than four thousand kilometres, navigated without instruments by Mau Piailug, one of the last fully trained navigators. The voyage was intended to test whether such journeys were possible at all. Its success settled the argument about accidental settlement, and Piailug subsequently broke with custom by teaching outsiders, on the grounds that the alternative was extinction.

Paragraph H
Today several hundred people have been trained in the revived tradition and traditional canoes have circumnavigated the globe. The knowledge is no longer at risk in the way it was fifty years ago. What remains striking is not that the system worked but that it was invented at all — a solution to one of the hardest navigational problems on earth, arrived at with no instrument more complex than a memorised sky.
